one_liner: Alpha MIR-based AngelScript JIT; author reports about 5x over the stock interpreter on call loops, 0-40% over BMS JIT.
what_it_does: angelsea plugs into an unmodified AngelScript 2.37.0+ engine through the asIJITCompilerV2 interface: set asEP_INCLUDE_JIT_INSTRUCTIONS, asEP_JIT_INTERFACE_VERSION 2 and asEP_BUILD_WITHOUT_LINE_CUES, construct angelsea::Jit with a JitConfig and call engine->SetJITCompiler. Scripts and bindings stay as they are; functions are compiled lazily after 15,000 JIT-entry hits by default (eager mode and an async compile callback exist), and any bytecode it cannot handle falls back to the interpreter at JIT entry points.
how_it_is_fast: A bytecode-to-C translator (bytecode2c) emits one C function per AngelScript function with VM field offsets baked in, and MIR's c2mir compiles that C in memory to machine code (MIR optimisation level 2). Most of the advertised win is call overhead: generated code calls registered generic functions directly with per-function pooled asCGeneric objects, has a direct native-call path with optional stack elision, and fast script call/return paths, skipping VM bookkeeping such as suspend checks and program/stack-pointer updates (the hack_ignore_* defaults).
when_to_use: An existing AngelScript-based game or app on 64-bit x86 (Linux gcc/clang, Windows MinGW or MSVC) whose scripts spend much time calling registered application functions, especially through asCALL_GENERIC.
You already use the BlindMindStudios JIT on 64-bit and want a maintained-ish replacement with better coverage; the author measured +0 to 40% over it on King Arthur's Gold.
Long-running scripted hot loops where lazy compilation keeps cold #included code out of the JIT and async compilation hides compile latency.
As a base for ahead-of-time translation of AngelScript to C (the bytecode2c output is plain C, though the README says AOT is not yet viable).
when_not_to_use: 32-bit x86, macOS x86-64 (fails CI, issue #3) or big-endian targets; aarch64 Linux and macOS are experimental and untested on a real app.
Engines that run AngelScript contexts on multiple threads: the README says the JIT is not thread-safe with multithreaded contexts or engines (issue #7 open).

Hosts that rely on suspending scripts (line callbacks, timeouts), on C++ exceptions thrown by registered functions, or on inspecting the calling context from native callbacks: the default hacks ignore all three during JIT execution.
Production builds that need stability guarantees: alpha quality, a downstream MIR fork required, async compile failures crash the app (issue #24 open), and no commits since 2025-09-16.
Huge script functions: MIR compile cost can reach gigabytes, so functions over 25,000 bytecode bytes are skipped by default.

integration.dependencies: AngelScript 2.37.0+ (asIJITCompilerV2), fmt, MIR via the asumagic/mir downstream fork; all vendored as git submodules; Catch2 and nanobench only for tests
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux (gcc, clang) and Windows (MinGW, MSVC); aarch64 Linux and macOS experimental; no 32-bit x86, no macOS x86-64, no big-endian
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe with multithreaded AngelScript contexts or engines (README, issue #7); asynchronous compilation is supported with one codegen thread at a time
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — attaches to the stock engine through asIJITCompilerV2 with three engine properties and no script changes, but requires AngelScript 2.37+, the 64-bit platforms above, line cues disabled, and accepting the default semantic hacks

gotchas: Harness note on the ~5x figure: the generic ABI benchmark (tests/abi.cpp, tests/scripts/abi.as) binds noarg to generic_noarg_hack and add_obj to generic_add_obj_hack, which write asCGeneric::returnVal and read stackPointer/currentObject directly through AngelScript's private as_generic.h header instead of the virtual asIScriptGeneric calls; with near-empty callees the loop measures pure call dispatch, the case the JIT optimises most, so ordinary generic bindings (GetArgDWord, SetReturnDWord) would show a smaller ratio. No results, CPU or compiler are committed for this or the native-ABI and brainfuck benchmarks.

The benchmark config is not the shipped default: tests use eager compilation and experimental_stack_elision = true, while the library defaults to lazy compilation after 15,000 hits and stack elision off.

Part of the speed comes from relaxed semantics enabled by default: hack_ignore_suspend (asBC_SUSPEND ignored, so script suspension and line-callback timeouts do not fire in JIT code), hack_ignore_exceptions (C++ exceptions from application functions are not handled on direct system calls) and hack_ignore_context_inspect (program and stack pointers not updated, breaking callees that use the debug interface; issue #26 tracks m_callingSystemFunction).

Upstream MIR miscompiles its code (GVN load/store optimisations, integer sign-extension issue #423, jump-optimisation use-after-free issue #424); the asumagic/mir fork works around them and the config warns that MIR level 3 is known broken.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick angelsea over the BlindMindStudios AngelScript JIT on 64-bit x86 or aarch64 with AngelScript 2.37+, since BMS is unmaintained, x86-only and falls back to the interpreter often per this README; keep BMS for 32-bit x86. Against switching the scripting language to Luau or Daslang it is the only option here that speeds up an existing AngelScript codebase in place.
verified_claims_summary: First-party only: the README's ~5x is the JIT versus the stock AngelScript interpreter in the same engine (interpreter module built without JIT instructions, both without line cues) on 1-million-iteration loops calling a near-empty registered generic function, timed with nanobench in relative mode, with no CPU, compiler, flags or results published. The +0 to 40% over the BlindMindStudios JIT comes from a private King Arthur's Gold dev build with no published workload or hardware.
status_note: Stale since 2025-09-16 (alpha, 12 open issues including crash-on-async-compile-failure #24 and multithreaded-context support #7) but BSD-2-Clause, CMake-vendorable with submodules, and exercised by its author on a commercial game's dev build.
